prompt: An RP algorithm never accepts a no-instance and accepts each yes-instance with probability at least one half. You repeat with fresh independent randomness and accept if any run accepts. What changes?

options.text: False positives appear as the number of runs grows
options.explanation: No individual run can accept a no-instance, so neither can their any-accept combination.

options.text: Missed yes-instances become less likely while no-instances remain certainly rejected
options.explanation: A miss now requires every independent run to miss.

options.text: The error bound stays unchanged because each run has the same bound
options.explanation: The combined error requires several independent failures, whose probabilities multiply.

options.text: Every yes-instance becomes certainly accepted after finitely many runs
options.explanation: The miss probability decreases but need not become zero.

workedExample: On a no-instance no run can accept, so any-accept never creates a false positive. On a yes-instance the combined procedure fails only if every independent trial misses. Fresh trials multiply the miss bounds. Repeating the identical random choices would not provide that improvement.

prompt: A BPP decision algorithm is right with probability two thirds. For three independent runs, which outcomes must be counted when bounding a wrong majority?

options.explanation: Exactly two wrong answers also form a wrong majority.

options.text: Exactly two wrong answers and three wrong answers
options.explanation: These are all ways a three-run majority can be incorrect.

options.text: Any outcome containing one wrong answer
options.explanation: One wrong answer is outvoted by two correct answers.

options.text: No outcomes: majority voting is always correct
options.explanation: Amplification reduces bounded error; it does not eliminate all error.

workedExample: With three runs the majority is wrong when exactly two or all three runs are wrong. Counting only unanimous errors omits the first case. Fresh independent trials with success bounded above one half make a wrong majority less likely; they do not make it impossible. Shared failures from repeating identical randomness cannot be treated as independent.
